claims.text: The target high-entropy nanoalloys contain multiple principal elements.
Deliberately introducing configurational disorder can improve the structural stability of high-entropy nanoalloys at high temperature.
Deliberately introducing configurational disorder can improve the chemical stability of high-entropy nanoalloys at high temperature.
Selecting elements with similar ionic radii introduces configurational disorder into high-entropy nanoalloys.
Promoting a single-phase solid solution introduces or maintains configurational disorder.
Configurational disorder produces a high-entropy effect.
The high-entropy effect can drive a reversible solid-state transformation between multiphase and single-phase states.
The reversible multiphase-to-single-phase transformation improves structural stability.
The reversible multiphase-to-single-phase transformation improves chemical stability.
Disorder-engineered high-entropy nanoalloys will be more structurally stable than otherwise comparable nanoalloys without deliberate disorder engineering.
Disorder-engineered high-entropy nanoalloys will be more chemically stable than otherwise comparable nanoalloys without deliberate disorder engineering.
The proposed stability improvement is expected to be significant at high temperatures.
The magnitude of the stability improvement may depend on alloy composition.
The magnitude of the stability improvement may depend on processing conditions.
The exact relationship between configurational disorder and stability improvement is not fully understood.
A controlled high-temperature comparison using X-ray diffraction, transmission electron microscopy, and thermal gravimetry can test the predicted stability difference.
The hypothesis is falsified if the control nanoalloys show stability similar to or better than the disorder-engineered nanoalloys.
